Seul le champ origine a été recherché (2026-10-06), dans les volumes UNESCO de l'Histoire générale de l'Afrique : chaque piste est attribuée et citée à la page, aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. oralTraditions.claim: The kings of Wagadu, the Sise, were early allies of Sunjata Keita, as were the kings of Nema.
oralTraditions.collector: Djibril Tamsir Niane, qui rapporte la tradition sans nommer son porteur
oralTraditions.context: Note from a historical synthesis published by UNESCO in 1985; neither the bearer, nor the place, nor the date of the collection is given.

historicalSyntheses.claim: The Sise ("Cissé") of Wagadu, who had become Muslims and political allies of Sunjata Keita, are among the five marabout clans that were early allies, proclaimed the "five guardians of the faith" by the assembly that organised the Mali empire.

In the time of the askia Mohammed, Sise ("Cissé") was a religious title, like Ture ("Touré"). The chapter notes this in connection with that ruler, of the Ture or Sylla clan, and gives no meaning for the word.
Among the oldest clans of Songhay society, of Soninke origin, are the Sise, together with the Ture, Sylla, Tunkara, Jakite, Drame and Jawara.

A reading of the history of Ghana, attributed to Delafosse, has the Black Soninke led, towards the end of the eighth century, by their first king (tunka), Kaya Maghan Cissé, who is said to have driven the White peoples back towards the Tagant, the Gorgol and the Futa. The chapter reports it in the conditional, in the midst of a review of the readings that explain the foundation of Ghana by founders who came from elsewhere.

sources.notes: This name appears in our coverage list: it was selected as a name to document, but no dedicated source has yet been consulted. The fiche therefore exists to flag the name, not for what it asserts about it. Forthcoming checks will draw on electoral rolls, national statistical institutes and onomastic studies of the country concerned.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, III : L'Afrique du VIIe au XIe siècle — chapitre 5, Les peuples du Soudan : mouvements de populations
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. M. El Fasi and I. Hrbek, 1990; chapter by F. de Medeiros. Printed page 153: the reading by Delafosse (1912, vol. II, p. 198 ff., after note 27) in which the Soninke are led by Kaya Maghan Cissé, their first king, towards the end of the eighth century, reported as an example of a diffusionist interpretation of the foundation of Ghana. Delafosse's original text has not been read. The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 6, Le Mali et la deuxième expansion manden
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by D. T. Niane. Printed pages: the five marabout clans that were early allies, among them the Sise of Wagadu, Islamised and political allies of Sunjata Keita (p. 158); note 45: the tradition says that the kings of Wagadu, the Sise, were early allies of Sunjata Keita (p. 159). The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, IV : L'Afrique du XIIe au XVIe siècle — chapitre 8, Les Songhay du XIIe au XVIe siècle
sources.notes: UNESCO, ed. D. T. Niane, 1985; chapter by S. M. Cissoko. Printed pages: note 13 on the askia Mohammed, of the Ture or Sylla clan, Ture being at that time a religious title just like Sise (p. 219); the oldest clans of Songhay society, of Soninke origin (Ture, Sylla, Tunkara, Sise, Jakite, Drame, Jawara) (p. 230). The chapter gives no meaning for the name.

gaps.reason: No meaning of the name Cissé is established in the sources we have consulted: they say where the clan is attested and what it did, not what the word means. The accounts and readings above are attributed leads; none is held to be the right one.
